text: Snowflake gives you a real, specific syntax for pulling a named field out of a VARIANT value: a colon to reach in, a double colon to cast. This lesson is about using both correctly, because skipping the cast is an easy mistake with real consequences down the line.

A colon alone, raw_payload colon ticket_id, returns the field, but it's still typed VARIANT, not a true string or number. Cast it explicitly with double colon: STRING, NUMBER of ten comma two, TIMESTAMP underscore NTZ. An uncast refund amount can look numeric in a results grid but sort and compare as semi-structured, not a true number — which quietly breaks a SUM or an ORDER BY later.

Here's the full preview: every field this pipeline needs, extracted and cast in one SELECT, run against the real landed data. This isn't a throwaway exploration query — it's the exact extraction logic Lesson 6's MERGE statement reuses field for field. Proving it here, on a query you can eyeball and rerun freely, is far cheaper than discovering a type mismatch inside a MERGE that's already wired to a scheduled task.

Not every row has every field populated. Snowflake's colon syntax returns SQL NULL automatically when a key is missing or its JSON value is null — no special-case syntax required. On most tickets, refund_amount simply lands NULL, because most tickets never involve a refund at all.
With the parsing logic proven, next lesson puts a Stream on the raw table — tracking exactly which rows are new since the last time anything read them, automatically.
